# Exercise 4.2 — The decision boundary {#sec-decision-boundary}

In Exercise 4.1 the map of the logistic regression's probability had a black
line across it: to one side the model says `yes`, to the other `no`. That line
is the **decision boundary**. In this exercise you work it out from the
coefficients, see why it is straight, and move it with the threshold.

We use the same people as Exercise 4.1: age, systolic blood
pressure, and whether they had a cardiovascular event in the next ten years.
Both measurements matter, so the boundary is tilted.

- **Part 1.** Find the boundary by hand from the coefficients, draw it, and
  see it in 3D as the line where the S-shaped probability sheet cuts the
  plane P = 0.5.
- **Part 2.** Change the threshold and see the line move: every threshold
  gives its own line.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## The plots are for looking at
The code for the plots is folded away under **Code for this plot
(optional)**. You do not need to write it, but it is in the download if you
want it.
:::

### Packages and data

```{r}
# Packages for this exercise. If one is missing, remove the # and run this line once:
# install.packages(c("tidyverse", "tidymodels", "plotly"))

library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)

theme_set(theme_bw())
```

`data/cvd_risk.csv` holds 500 adults aged 40 to 80 seen at a health check:
their age, their systolic blood pressure in mmHg, and whether they had a
cardiovascular event (a heart attack or a stroke) in the following ten years.
If you do not have it yet, [**download `cvd_risk.csv`**](data/cvd_risk.csv){download="cvd_risk.csv"}
into your `data` folder.

```{r}
cvd <- read_csv("data/cvd_risk.csv") |>
  mutate(cvd = factor(cvd, levels = c("no", "yes")))

set.seed(42)
split <- initial_split(cvd, prop = 0.8)
train <- training(split)
test  <- testing(split)

count(train, cvd)
```

### Part 1 — Where the class changes

Fit a logistic regression with both measurements, the same way as in
Exercise 4.1:

```{r}
log_model <- logistic_reg() |>
  set_engine("glm") |>
  set_mode("classification")

log_fit <- log_model |>
  fit(cvd ~ age + systolic_bp, data = train)

b <- log_fit$fit$coefficients      # intercept, age, blood pressure
b
```

The model is a straight line on the **log-odds** scale. Log-odds are another
way of writing a probability $p$: $\log\big(p / (1 - p)\big)$. A probability of
0.5 has log-odds 0; higher probabilities have positive log-odds, lower ones
negative. The sigmoid turns log-odds back into a probability.


$$\text{log-odds} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{age} + \beta_2 \times \text{blood pressure}$$

By default the model says `yes` when the probability is 0.5 or more. At 0.5
the probability is shared equally between the two classes: 0.5 for an event and
0.5 for no event. Above it `yes` is the more likely class, below it `no`. So
the class changes where the probability is 0.5, which is **log-odds of 0**. So the boundary is every
combination of age and blood pressure where

$$\beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{age} + \beta_2 \times \text{blood pressure} = 0$$

For a given blood pressure, solve for age:

$$\text{age} = \frac{-\beta_0 - \beta_2 \times \text{blood pressure}}{\beta_1}$$

#### Task 1a — The boundary at a blood pressure of 120 and of 160

Round the coefficients printed above to four significant figures and calculate,
by hand, the age at which the class changes for a blood pressure of 120 mmHg.
Then do the same for 160 mmHg.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
boundary_120 <- (-(______) - ______ * 120) / ______
boundary_160 <- (-(______) - ______ * 160) / ______
c(boundary_120, boundary_160)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
In order: the intercept, the blood-pressure weight, and the age weight. The
intercept is negative, so minus the intercept is a positive number.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
boundary_120 <- (-(-13.83) - 0.05083 * 120) / 0.1019
boundary_160 <- (-(-13.83) - 0.05083 * 160) / 0.1019
c(boundary_120, boundary_160)
```

With a blood pressure of 120 the model predicts an event from about age 76;
with 160, from about age 56.
:::
:::

Check it with `predict()`: a person on the boundary should get a probability
of 0.5.

```{r}
predict(log_fit, new_data = data.frame(age = 75.9, systolic_bp = 120), type = "prob")
```

Every point on the boundary satisfies one linear equation in age and blood
pressure, so the boundary is a **straight line**. Here it is, drawn from the
coefficients, over the test patients:

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
# the boundary written as blood pressure = a + s * age
ggplot(test, aes(x = age, y = systolic_bp, shape = cvd, colour = cvd)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_abline(intercept = -b[1] / b[3], slope = -b[2] / b[3], linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("point", x = c(75.9, 55.9), y = c(120, 160), colour = "red", size = 3) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(no = 1, yes = 17)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(no = "steelblue", yes = "darkorange")) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(40, 80), ylim = c(80, 200)) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Systolic blood pressure (mmHg)",
       shape = "Event", colour = "Event",
       title = "The decision boundary at a threshold of 0.5")
```

Above and to the right of the line the model says `yes`; below and to the left,
`no`. The line is tilted because both measurements count: an older person
needs a lower blood pressure to cross it.

#### The same line in three dimensions

The model turns age and blood pressure into a probability with the sigmoid.
Drawn above the age–blood pressure floor, that probability is an S-shaped
**sheet** between 0 and 1. The flat grey plane is the level P = 0.5. The
decision boundary, the black line, is nothing more than where the sheet cuts
through that plane: where the sheet is above the plane the model says `yes`,
where it is below, `no`. Seen from above, it is the line you drew in Task 1a.
Turn the plot with the mouse and scroll to zoom.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
#| eval: !expr requireNamespace("plotly", quietly = TRUE)
# This plot needs the plotly package: install.packages("plotly")
ages <- seq(40, 80, by = 1)
bps  <- seq(80, 200, by = 2)

# the probability at every grid point (one row per blood pressure, one column
# per age): the sigmoid of the log-odds
logodds_matrix <- outer(bps, ages, function(s, a) b[1] + b[2] * a + b[3] * s)
prob_matrix <- 1 / (1 + exp(-logodds_matrix))

# the boundary: the age where the probability is 0.5 (log-odds 0), for each blood pressure
line_age <- (-b[1] - b[3] * bps) / b[2]
on_floor <- line_age >= 40 & line_age <= 80

plotly::plot_ly() |>
  plotly::add_surface(x = ages, y = bps, z = prob_matrix, opacity = 0.75,
                      colorscale = list(c(0, 1), c("steelblue", "darkorange")),
                      showscale = FALSE, name = "probability") |>
  plotly::add_surface(x = ages, y = bps, z = 0 * prob_matrix + 0.5, opacity = 0.4,
                      colorscale = list(c(0, 1), c("grey", "grey")), showscale = FALSE,
                      name = "P = 0.5") |>
  plotly::add_trace(type = "scatter3d", mode = "lines", x = line_age[on_floor],
                    y = bps[on_floor], z = rep(0.5, sum(on_floor)),
                    line = list(color = "black", width = 8), name = "boundary at 0.5") |>
  plotly::layout(scene = list(xaxis = list(title = "Age (years)"),
                              yaxis = list(title = "Systolic BP (mmHg)"),
                              zaxis = list(title = "Probability of an event")))
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
if (!requireNamespace("plotly", quietly = TRUE)) knitr::asis_output(paste0(
  "*The plot you can turn is missing from this copy of the page: it needs the R ",
  "package `plotly`. Run `install.packages(\"plotly\")` and render again.*"))
```

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Think about it
1. As far as the model is concerned, 10 mmHg more blood pressure is worth how
   many years of age? Where do you see that in the plot?
2. Two people: one is 70 with a blood pressure of 128, the other 55 with 165.
   Which side of the line is each on?
3. A model with three predictors (say age, blood pressure and cholesterol) also
   has a boundary. What shape would it be?
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
predict(log_fit, new_data = data.frame(age = c(70, 55), systolic_bp = c(128, 165)),
        type = "prob")
```

1. About 5 years: 10 × 0.0508 / 0.1019 = 5.0. Adding 10 mmHg raises the
   log-odds as much as 5 extra years. That is the tilt of the line: going 10
   mmHg up, the boundary moves 5 years younger (from 76 at 120 mmHg to 56 at
   160 mmHg).
2. The 70-year-old is just below the line (probability 0.45, `no`); the
   55-year-old is above it (0.54, `yes`). The younger person is called `yes`
   because of the blood pressure. Neither measurement decides alone.
3. Still flat: one linear equation in three measurements is a flat plane in
   three dimensions. A logistic regression always has a flat boundary in the
   predictors you give it.
:::
:::

### Part 2 — Other thresholds, other lines

The cut-off of 0.5 is called the **decision threshold**. Nothing forces it to
be 0.5: we could call someone `yes` from a probability of 0.3, or only from
0.7. Each threshold gives its own line. Each line is where the S-shaped sheet
of Part 1 is cut by a flat plane at that height: the plane at 0.3 sits lower
and cuts the sheet at younger ages and lower blood pressures; the plane at 0.7
sits higher and cuts it further up. Seen from above, the three lines are
parallel: the same tilt, shifted.

On the left, the sheet with the three planes (turn it with the mouse); on the
right, the same three lines seen from above, in the same colours.

:::: {layout-ncol="2"}
```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for the 3D plot (optional)"
#| eval: !expr requireNamespace("plotly", quietly = TRUE)
# uses ages, bps and prob_matrix from the 3D plot in Part 1
thresholds <- c(0.3, 0.5, 0.7)
colours    <- c("blue", "red", "purple")

planes_3d <- plotly::plot_ly() |>
  plotly::add_surface(x = ages, y = bps, z = prob_matrix, opacity = 0.6,
                      colorscale = list(c(0, 1), c("steelblue", "darkorange")),
                      showscale = FALSE, name = "probability")

for (i in 1:3) {
  t <- thresholds[i]
  # the age where the probability equals t, for each blood pressure
  cut_age <- (log(t / (1 - t)) - b[1] - b[3] * bps) / b[2]
  keep <- cut_age >= 40 & cut_age <= 80
  planes_3d <- planes_3d |>
    plotly::add_surface(x = ages, y = bps, z = 0 * prob_matrix + t, opacity = 0.25,
                        colorscale = list(c(0, 1), c(colours[i], colours[i])),
                        showscale = FALSE, name = paste("P =", t)) |>
    plotly::add_trace(type = "scatter3d", mode = "lines", x = cut_age[keep],
                      y = bps[keep], z = rep(t, sum(keep)),
                      line = list(color = colours[i], width = 8),
                      name = paste("threshold", t))
}

planes_3d |>
  plotly::layout(scene = list(xaxis = list(title = "Age (years)"),
                              yaxis = list(title = "Systolic BP (mmHg)"),
                              zaxis = list(title = "Probability of an event")),
                 legend = list(orientation = "h"))
```

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
lines_t <- data.frame(t = factor(c(0.3, 0.5, 0.7)),
                      log_odds = log(c(0.3, 0.5, 0.7) / (1 - c(0.3, 0.5, 0.7)))) |>
  mutate(intercept = (log_odds - b[1]) / b[3], slope = -b[2] / b[3])

ggplot(test, aes(x = age, y = systolic_bp)) +
  geom_point(aes(shape = cvd), size = 2, colour = "grey30") +
  geom_abline(data = lines_t, aes(intercept = intercept, slope = slope, colour = t),
              linewidth = 1) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(no = 1, yes = 17)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("0.3" = "blue", "0.5" = "red", "0.7" = "purple")) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(40, 80), ylim = c(80, 200)) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Systolic blood pressure (mmHg)",
       shape = "Event", colour = "Threshold",
       title = "Three thresholds, three parallel boundaries")
```
::::

::: {.callout-important}
## Key idea
We could have picked another threshold, and we would have had a different line
separating our classes in 2D: one line for each threshold. The 0.5 line,
where both classes are equally likely, is only the default.
:::

Everyone above a line is predicted `yes` at that threshold. Count them:

```{r}
test_probs <- predict(log_fit, new_data = test, type = "prob")$.pred_yes

c(t_0.3 = sum(test_probs >= 0.3), t_0.5 = sum(test_probs >= 0.5),
  t_0.7 = sum(test_probs >= 0.7))
```

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Think about it
Lowering the threshold from 0.5 to 0.3 calls many more test patients `yes`.
On the plot, which patients change side when the line moves from 0.5 to 0.3:
triangles (they had an event), circles (they did not), or both?
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
50 patients are called `yes` at 0.3, 34 at 0.5 and 17 at 0.7. Moving the line
down (0.3) brings more of the triangles onto the `yes` side, but it brings over
circles too. Moving it up (0.7) does the opposite: fewer circles called `yes`,
but more triangles missed. The model, its coefficients and the tilt of the line
are the same; only the decision changed. Why you might want to move it is the
subject of Exercise 4.3.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Learning points
- The decision boundary is where the predicted probability equals the
  threshold: where the S-shaped sheet cuts a flat plane at that height. At
  0.5 the two classes are equally likely, and the log-odds are 0.
- A logistic regression's boundary is straight (flat) in its predictors.
  Another threshold gives another, parallel line: the same tilt, shifted.
:::

### Packages and data

```{python}
# Packages for this exercise. If one is missing, install it once from a terminal
# (in a Jupyter notebook, type %pip instead of pip):
# pip install pandas numpy matplotlib scikit-learn plotly

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, export_text
```

`data/cvd_risk.csv` holds 500 adults aged 40 to 80 seen at a health check:
their age, their systolic blood pressure in mmHg, and whether they had a
cardiovascular event (a heart attack or a stroke) in the following ten years.
If you do not have it yet, [**download `cvd_risk.csv`**](data/cvd_risk.csv){download="cvd_risk.csv"}
into your `data` folder.

```{python}
cvd = pd.read_csv("data/cvd_risk.csv")

train, test = train_test_split(cvd, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)

train["cvd"].value_counts()
```

### Part 1 — Where the class changes

Fit a logistic regression with both measurements, the same way as in
Exercise 4.1:

```{python}
log_model = LogisticRegression(C=np.inf)
log_model.fit(train[["age", "systolic_bp"]], train["cvd"])

b0 = log_model.intercept_[0]
b1, b2 = log_model.coef_[0]          # age, blood pressure
print("intercept:", b0)
print("weights (age, blood pressure):", b1, b2)
```

The model is a straight line on the **log-odds** scale. Log-odds are another
way of writing a probability $p$: $\log\big(p / (1 - p)\big)$. A probability of
0.5 has log-odds 0; higher probabilities have positive log-odds, lower ones
negative. The sigmoid turns log-odds back into a probability.


$$\text{log-odds} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{age} + \beta_2 \times \text{blood pressure}$$

By default the model says `yes` when the probability is 0.5 or more. At 0.5
the probability is shared equally between the two classes: 0.5 for an event and
0.5 for no event. Above it `yes` is the more likely class, below it `no`. So
the class changes where the probability is 0.5, which is **log-odds of 0**. So the boundary is every
combination of age and blood pressure where

$$\beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{age} + \beta_2 \times \text{blood pressure} = 0$$

For a given blood pressure, solve for age:

$$\text{age} = \frac{-\beta_0 - \beta_2 \times \text{blood pressure}}{\beta_1}$$

#### Task 1a — The boundary at a blood pressure of 120 and of 160

Round the coefficients printed above to four significant figures and calculate,
by hand, the age at which the class changes for a blood pressure of 120 mmHg.
Then do the same for 160 mmHg.

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
boundary_120 = (-(______) - ______ * 120) / ______
boundary_160 = (-(______) - ______ * 160) / ______
print(boundary_120, boundary_160)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
In order: the intercept, the blood-pressure weight, and the age weight. The
intercept is negative, so minus the intercept is a positive number.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
boundary_120 = (-(-15.06) - 0.05366 * 120) / 0.1159
boundary_160 = (-(-15.06) - 0.05366 * 160) / 0.1159
print(boundary_120, boundary_160)
```

With a blood pressure of 120 the model predicts an event from about age 74;
with 160, from about age 56.
:::
:::

Check it with `.predict_proba()`: a person on the boundary should get a
probability of 0.5.

```{python}
log_model.predict_proba(pd.DataFrame({"age": [74.4], "systolic_bp": [120]}))
```

Every point on the boundary satisfies one linear equation in age and blood
pressure, so the boundary is a **straight line**. Here it is, drawn from the
coefficients, over the test patients:

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
age_line = np.array([40, 80])
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for cls, mk, colour in [("no", "o", "steelblue"), ("yes", "^", "darkorange")]:
    rows = test[test["cvd"] == cls]
    ax.scatter(rows["age"], rows["systolic_bp"], marker=mk, color=colour, s=20, label=cls)
# the boundary written as blood pressure = (-b0 - b1 * age) / b2
ax.plot(age_line, (-b0 - b1 * age_line) / b2, color="black", linewidth=2)
ax.scatter([74.4, 55.9], [120, 160], color="red", s=50, zorder=3)
ax.set_xlim(40, 80)
ax.set_ylim(80, 200)
ax.set_xlabel("Age (years)")
ax.set_ylabel("Systolic blood pressure (mmHg)")
ax.legend(title="Event")
ax.set_title("The decision boundary at a threshold of 0.5")
plt.show()
```

Above and to the right of the line the model says `yes`; below and to the left,
`no`. The line is tilted because both measurements count: an older person
needs a lower blood pressure to cross it.

#### The same line in three dimensions

The model turns age and blood pressure into a probability with the sigmoid.
Drawn above the age–blood pressure floor, that probability is an S-shaped
**sheet** between 0 and 1. The flat grey plane is the level P = 0.5. The
decision boundary, the black line, is nothing more than where the sheet cuts
through that plane: where the sheet is above the plane the model says `yes`,
where it is below, `no`. Seen from above, it is the line you drew in Task 1a.
Turn the plot with the mouse and scroll to zoom.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
#| eval: false
# This plot needs the plotly package: pip install plotly
import plotly.graph_objects as go

ages = np.arange(40, 81, 1)
bps = np.arange(80, 201, 2)
A, S = np.meshgrid(ages, bps)

# the probability at every grid point (one row per blood pressure, one column
# per age): the sigmoid of the log-odds
logodds_matrix = b0 + b1 * A + b2 * S
prob_matrix = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-logodds_matrix))

# the boundary: the age where the probability is 0.5 (log-odds 0), for each blood pressure
line_age = (-b0 - b2 * bps) / b1
on_floor = (line_age >= 40) & (line_age <= 80)

fig_prob = go.Figure()
fig_prob.add_trace(go.Surface(x=ages, y=bps, z=prob_matrix, opacity=0.75,
    colorscale=[[0, "steelblue"], [1, "darkorange"]], showscale=False, name="probability"))
fig_prob.add_trace(go.Surface(x=ages, y=bps, z=0 * prob_matrix + 0.5, opacity=0.4,
    colorscale=[[0, "grey"], [1, "grey"]], showscale=False, name="P = 0.5"))
fig_prob.add_trace(go.Scatter3d(x=line_age[on_floor], y=bps[on_floor],
    z=np.full(on_floor.sum(), 0.5), mode="lines", line={"color": "black", "width": 8},
    name="boundary at 0.5"))
fig_prob.update_layout(scene={"xaxis_title": "Age (years)",
                              "yaxis_title": "Systolic BP (mmHg)",
                              "zaxis_title": "Probability of an event"})
fig_prob.show()
```

## Think about it
1. As far as the model is concerned, 10 mmHg more blood pressure is worth how
   many years of age? Where do you see that in the plot?
2. Two people: one is 70 with a blood pressure of 128, the other 55 with 165.
   Which side of the line is each on?
3. A model with three predictors (say age, blood pressure and cholesterol) also
   has a boundary. What shape would it be?
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
log_model.predict_proba(pd.DataFrame({"age": [70, 55], "systolic_bp": [128, 165]}))
```

1. About 5 years: 10 × 0.0537 / 0.1159 = 4.6. Adding 10 mmHg raises the
   log-odds as much as 5 extra years. That is the tilt of the line: going 10
   mmHg up, the boundary moves 5 years younger (from 74 at 120 mmHg to 56 at
   160 mmHg).
2. The 70-year-old is just below the line (probability 0.48, `no`); the
   55-year-old is above it (0.54, `yes`). The younger person is called `yes`
   because of the blood pressure. Neither measurement decides alone.
3. Still flat: one linear equation in three measurements is a flat plane in
   three dimensions. A logistic regression always has a flat boundary in the
   predictors you give it.
:::
:::

### Part 2 — Other thresholds, other lines

The cut-off of 0.5 is called the **decision threshold**. Nothing forces it to
be 0.5: we could call someone `yes` from a probability of 0.3, or only from
0.7. Each threshold gives its own line. Each line is where the S-shaped sheet
of Part 1 is cut by a flat plane at that height: the plane at 0.3 sits lower
and cuts the sheet at younger ages and lower blood pressures; the plane at 0.7
sits higher and cuts it further up. Seen from above, the three lines are
parallel: the same tilt, shifted.

On the left, the sheet with the three planes (turn it with the mouse); on the
right, the same three lines seen from above, in the same colours.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for the 3D plot (optional)"
#| eval: false
# This plot needs the plotly package: pip install plotly
# uses ages, bps and prob_matrix from the 3D plot in Part 1
fig_planes = go.Figure()
fig_planes.add_trace(go.Surface(x=ages, y=bps, z=prob_matrix, opacity=0.6,
    colorscale=[[0, "steelblue"], [1, "darkorange"]], showscale=False, name="probability"))
for t, colour in [(0.3, "blue"), (0.5, "red"), (0.7, "purple")]:
    # the age where the probability equals t, for each blood pressure
    cut_age = (np.log(t / (1 - t)) - b0 - b2 * bps) / b1
    keep = (cut_age >= 40) & (cut_age <= 80)
    fig_planes.add_trace(go.Surface(x=ages, y=bps, z=0 * prob_matrix + t, opacity=0.25,
        colorscale=[[0, colour], [1, colour]], showscale=False, name=f"P = {t}"))
    fig_planes.add_trace(go.Scatter3d(x=cut_age[keep], y=bps[keep],
        z=np.full(keep.sum(), t), mode="lines", line={"color": colour, "width": 8},
        name=f"threshold {t}"))
fig_planes.update_layout(scene={"xaxis_title": "Age (years)",
                                "yaxis_title": "Systolic BP (mmHg)",
                                "zaxis_title": "Probability of an event"},
                         legend={"orientation": "h"})
fig_planes.show()
```

#| echo: false
# Draws the Python model's sheet and planes (values from the Python cells above).
if (requireNamespace("plotly", quietly = TRUE)) {

  colours    <- c("blue", "red", "purple")

                        colorscale = list(c(0, 1), c("steelblue", "darkorange")),
                        showscale = FALSE, name = "probability")
  for (i in 1:3) {
    t <- thresholds[i]
    cut_age <- (log(t / (1 - t)) - P$b0 - P$b2 * P$bps) / P$b1
    keep <- cut_age >= 40 & cut_age <= 80
    planes_3d <- planes_3d |>
      plotly::add_surface(x = P$ages, y = P$bps, z = 0 * P$prob_matrix + t, opacity = 0.25,
                          colorscale = list(c(0, 1), c(colours[i], colours[i])),
                          showscale = FALSE, name = paste("P =", t)) |>
      plotly::add_trace(type = "scatter3d", mode = "lines", x = cut_age[keep],
                        y = P$bps[keep], z = rep(t, sum(keep)),
                        line = list(color = colours[i], width = 8),
                        name = paste("threshold", t))
  }
  planes_3d |>
    plotly::layout(scene = list(xaxis = list(title = "Age (years)"),
                                yaxis = list(title = "Systolic BP (mmHg)"),
                                zaxis = list(title = "Probability of an event")),

} else knitr::asis_output(paste0(

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for this plot (optional)"
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for cls, mk in [("no", "o"), ("yes", "^")]:
    rows = test[test["cvd"] == cls]
    ax.scatter(rows["age"], rows["systolic_bp"], marker=mk, color="grey", s=20, label=cls)
for t, colour in [(0.3, "blue"), (0.5, "red"), (0.7, "purple")]:
    lo = np.log(t / (1 - t))
    ax.plot(age_line, (lo - b0 - b1 * age_line) / b2, color=colour,
            linewidth=2, label=f"threshold {t}")
ax.set_xlim(40, 80)
ax.set_ylim(80, 200)
ax.set_xlabel("Age (years)")
ax.set_ylabel("Systolic blood pressure (mmHg)")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
ax.set_title("Three thresholds, three parallel boundaries")
plt.show()
```
::::

::: {.callout-important}
## Key idea
We could have picked another threshold, and we would have had a different line
separating our classes in 2D: one line for each threshold. The 0.5 line,
where both classes are equally likely, is only the default.
:::

Everyone above a line is predicted `yes` at that threshold. Count them:

```{python}
test_probs = log_model.predict_proba(test[["age", "systolic_bp"]])[:, 1]

print("t = 0.3:", (test_probs >= 0.3).sum())
print("t = 0.5:", (test_probs >= 0.5).sum())
print("t = 0.7:", (test_probs >= 0.7).sum())
```

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Think about it
Lowering the threshold from 0.5 to 0.3 calls many more test patients `yes`.
On the plot, which patients change side when the line moves from 0.5 to 0.3:
triangles (they had an event), circles (they did not), or both?
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
40 patients are called `yes` at 0.3, 27 at 0.5 and 14 at 0.7. Moving the line
down (0.3) brings more of the triangles onto the `yes` side, but it brings over
circles too. Moving it up (0.7) does the opposite: fewer circles called `yes`,
but more triangles missed. The model, its coefficients and the tilt of the line
are the same; only the decision changed. Why you might want to move it is the
subject of Exercise 4.3.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Learning points
- The decision boundary is where the predicted probability equals the
  threshold: where the S-shaped sheet cuts a flat plane at that height. At
  0.5 the two classes are equally likely, and the log-odds are 0.
- A logistic regression's boundary is straight (flat) in its predictors.
  Another threshold gives another, parallel line: the same tilt, shifted.
:::

::: {.instructor}
**Teaching choice.** Part 1 links the map students saw in Exercise 4.1 to the
coefficients; Part 2 introduces the threshold, which Exercise 4.3 then puts
to use. No sensitivity or specificity here: that is Exercise 4.3. Both parts use the Day 4 dataset (`data/cvd_risk.csv`, simulated), in
which age and blood pressure carry similar weight, so the boundary is clearly
tilted. It is generated in `scripts/make_data.R` and described in
`data/PROVENANCE.txt`.

**Expected values.** Random split (R `set.seed(42)` + `initial_split(prop =
0.8)`; Python `train_test_split(test_size=0.2, random_state=42)`), so the two
languages differ. **R:** −13.83, age 0.1019, blood pressure 0.05083; boundary:
blood pressure = 272.1 − 2.006 × age; age 75.9 at 120 mmHg, 55.9 at 160 mmHg;
10 mmHg ≈ 5.0 years. Age 70 / BP 128: 0.453 `no`; age 55 / BP 165: 0.541 `yes`.
Thresholds 0.3, 0.5, 0.7 (log-odds −0.847, 0, 0.847, used only in the folded
plot code): age at 140 mmHg 57.5,
65.9, 74.2; test patients called `yes` 50, 34, 17. **Python:** −15.06, 0.1159,
0.05366; age 74.4 at 120 mmHg, 55.9 at 160 mmHg; 10 mmHg ≈ 4.6 years. Age 70 /
BP 128: 0.481 `no`; age 55 / BP 165: 0.542 `yes`. Age at 140 mmHg 57.8, 65.1,
72.4; test patients called `yes` 40, 27, 14.

**Common failures.** (1) Forgetting that the boundary uses log-odds 0, not
probability 0, and solving β0 + β1 age + β2 BP = 0.5. (2) Dropping the
minus sign of the intercept in Task 1a.

**Timing.** Part 1 twenty minutes, Part 2 ten.
:::
